heroText: Nuuk works best as a base in Greenland when you anchor days around Nuuk fjord, Greenland National Museum and Katuaq. Use those sights to understand the city's history, street life and visitor rhythm. Nuuk International Airport handles the main arrival flow, so hotel choice should balance the centre, transfer time and day-trip plans.

history.label: 2200 BC
history.text: The area around Nuuk was first occupied by the ancient, pre-Inuit, Paleo-Eskimo people of the Saqqaq culture as far back as 2200 BCE, when they lived in the area around the now abandoned settlement of Qoornoq.
For a long time, it was occupied by the Dorset culture around the former settlement of Kangeq, but they disappeared from the Nuuk district before 1000 AD.

history.label: 15th century
history.text: The Nuuk area was then inhabited by Norse settlers from around 1000 until the disappearance of the settlement for uncertain reasons during the 15th century.

The city proper was founded as the fort of Godt-Haab in 1728 by the royal governor Claus Paarss, when he relocated the missionary and merchant Hans Egede's earlier Hope Colony (Haabets Koloni) from Kangeq Island to the mainland.
Hans Egede returned to Denmark in 1736 after 15 years in Greenland, leaving his son Poul to continue his work.
In response, in 1861, he started the Atuagagdliutit, Greenland's first newspaper, with a native Greenlander as editor.

Godthaab became the seat of government for the Danish colony of South Greenland, while Godhavn (modern Qeqertarsuaq) was the capital of North Greenland until 1940, when the administration was unified in Godthaab.
Under new regulations in 1950, two councils amalgamated into one.
